findings.paper_title: Appendix A for External Auditors Annual Audit Report 2025/26
findings.headline: General Fund reserves are forecast to decline from £2.5m to £1.2m by 2028/29, cutting the council's buffer by half.
findings.detail: The council's cash reserves are forecast to fall to £1.2m by March 2029 from £2.5m in 2026/27, a decline of £1.3m (52%) over two years. The auditor notes reserves are 'forecast to continue declining' and this represents 'the most significant risks to its medium-term financial resilience'. The council's prior-year recommendation to rebuild reserves remains 'partially addressed'; the council has approved a Reserves Policy but has not yet set a minimum threshold and continues to forecast depletion rather than rebuilding.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce the council's capacity to absorb unexpected costs, shocks or slippage in income or savings delivery. At £1.2m, general reserves represent only 7% of net cost of service—a thin buffer for a council with £10m+ homelessness costs and a £35m contingent loan exposure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for External Auditors Annual Audit Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Council's loan exposure to housing company reached £35.6 million with maturity March 2028 and no homes sold to date.
findings.detail: The Council's loans to Rother DC Housing Company (RDCHC) increased from £9.8m to £33.0m (£35.6m including accrued interest) during the year, funded through external borrowing. Repayment depends on completion and sale of 200 homes; as at 31 March 2026 only three had been completed and none sold. As at July 2026 still no sales had been achieved, though seven are forecast in 2026/27. The loan matures in 28 months. RDCHC losses reached £2.11m in 2025/26, cumulative losses £6.9m. The auditor has raised a new recommendation to strengthen oversight and monitoring of the company's delivery and loan repayment capacity.
findings.matters: This is a contingent liquidity risk. The council borrowed externally to lend to a development company whose ability to repay depends on home sales in a weak housing market. If sales slip further, the council will either have to refinance maturing debt without the expected repayment, or use reserves. With only 28 months to maturity and zero sales recorded to July 2026, this is a live and material exposure.
findings.figures: £35.6m loan exposure (including accrued interest) maturing 31 March 2028; only 3 of 200 planned homes completed; zero sales as at July 2026; RDCHC annual losses £2.11m in 2025/26, cumulative losses £6.9m
findings.quote: The Council's financial exposure to Rother DC Housing Company Ltd (RDCHC) has increased materially to approximately £35.6 million and is funded through external borrowing. The loan agreement has a maturity date of 31 March 2028, with repayment largely dependent on the successful completion and sale of development units. As at 31 March 2026, only three of the planned 200 homes had been completed. Whilst seven open-market sales are forecast during 2026/27 and overall construction completion is expected by September 2027, no homes had been sold as at July 2026.

findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's ability to balance its budget without drawing reserves would be concerned at the combination of deteriorating savings delivery and continued reliance on reserves. The repeated miss signals either that budget-setting assumptions are too optimistic or that delivery capacity is weak—both risks to financial control.

findings.headline: £33.03m housing company investment at peak debt position with acknowledged risks
findings.detail: The council has invested £33.03m in its Housing Company (RDCHC), increasing by £23.5m during 2025/26 with a Development Facility Agreement formalized in March 2025. The housing company also owes the council £2.595m in accrued interest. Risk management section explicitly flags concerns with this investment during peak debt.
findings.matters: A £33m concentrated exposure to a development project undertaken at peak debt multiplies leverage and creates dependence on housing company performance for interest serviceability and capital repayment.
findings.figures: £33.03m invested, £23.5m increase in year, £2.595m accrued interest owed
findings.quote: Members are aware of the risks associated with the investment in RDCHC, especially as we reach the peak debt position and the interest has been accrued for.

findings.headline: Total council debt nearly doubled in one year to £53.5m through two large PWLB loans
findings.detail: Outstanding loans rose from £28.8m at the end of 2024/25 to £53.5m at 31 March 2026—an increase of £24.7m. This new borrowing comprised two Public Works Loan Board loans of £12.5m and £15.0m respectively, making it a near-doubling of the council's debt within a single financial year.
findings.matters: Near-doubling of debt in one year significantly increases financial leverage, repayment obligations, and interest rate risk exposure—material factors for credit assessment.
findings.figures: £53.5m total debt (from £28.8m), £24.7m increase, £12.5m and £15.0m new loans
findings.quote: The value of outstanding loans as at 31 March 2026 was £53.5m (compared to £28.8m at the end of 2024/25) and the borrowing portfolio is also shown in Appendix B. The Council's debt has increased by £24.7m since the start of the year, at year end this was largely represented by two new Public Works Loan Board loans of £12.5 and £15.0m respectively.

findings.headline: Debt servicing cost ratio jumped sevenfold to 8.13% of revenue from budgeted 1.1%
findings.detail: The ratio of Net Financing Costs to net revenue stream increased dramatically from a forecast 1.1% to an actual 8.13% in 2025/26. This reflects the impact of substantial new borrowing undertaken during the year as the council took on £24.7m in new loans.
findings.matters: A sevenfold increase in the proportion of revenue consumed by debt servicing materially affects financial sustainability and repayment capacity—key factors in lending decisions.
findings.figures: 1.1% forecast, 8.13% outturn
findings.quote: The ratio of Net Financing Costs (NFC) to the Net Revenue Stream in the original budget was forecast to be 1.1%. The outturn position was 8.13%

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand increased due to high rental costs, house prices, cost of living and constrained housing supply
findings.detail: Risk 2 reflects sharply increased homelessness driven by high rental costs, house prices, and the cost of living crisis, combined with constrained housing supply. Escalating costs continue despite mitigations.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a volatile, demand-driven cost that councils cannot easily control or predict, consuming reserves and reducing budget flexibility.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this excerpt
findings.quote: Risk 2 – Financial – The high costs of rental accommodation, house prices and living expenses are increasing demands for temporary accommodation. This score exceeds the risk appetite due to increased levels of homelessness and escalating costs.

findings.headline: Four major capital schemes face cost escalation - Project delivery risk increased from 8 to 12
findings.detail: Project delivery and cost control risks have worsened due to rising costs for services and construction, particularly on four major capital schemes. Mitigations are in place but cost pressures are evident and growing.
findings.matters: Cost overruns on capital projects consume reserves or require additional borrowing, reducing financial flexibility at a time when the council already faces sustainability challenges.
findings.figures: Risk rating increased from 8 to 12
findings.quote: Risk 4 – Project/Programme – Project delivery compromised and project budgets exceeded. This score has increased from 8 to 12 as costs for services and construction are increasing, especially around four of the Council's major capital schemes.

findings.headline: Housing company risk increased to highest rating (25) due to lack of sales in stagnant housing market
findings.detail: Rother DC Housing Company's risk rating has increased from 20 to 25 (highest) because the stagnant housing market has prevented sales. The confidential shareholder report scheduled for 22 July 2026 will provide further detail.
findings.matters: A council-owned company unable to trade in its core market represents both a revenue drain and potential requirement for council support or rescue borrowing.
findings.figures: Risk rating increased from 20 to 25
findings.quote: Risk 10 – Financial risk concerning the Rother DC Housing Company; the risk rating has increased from 20 to 25, the highest risk rating, considering the lack of sales caused by the stagnant housing market.

findings.headline: Financial sustainability risk rating increased to 25, the highest possible rating, reflecting pressure to operate within sustainable budget
findings.detail: The council's risk rating for failing to maintain a sustainable budget and adequate reserves has increased to 25, the highest possible rating. This reflects financial pressure the council faces even with mitigations in place and explicitly exceeds the council's own risk appetite threshold.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand why the council cannot meet its own financial sustainability threshold and what capacity remains for debt servicing.
findings.figures: Risk rating: 25 (highest)
findings.quote: Risk 3 – Economic/Financial – Failure to operate within a sustainable budget and hold adequate financial reserves. This score has increased to 25 which is the highest risk rating and reflects the financial pressure that the Council is under, even with mitigations in place.

findings.headline: Multiple savings delayed by capacity constraints — taxbase review, housing repairs, staffing efficiencies postponed
findings.detail: Three savings were not progressed due to capacity issues: the single persons discount taxbase review (£24,553, postponed to 26/27); in-house repair resource for temporary accommodation (£35,000, not yet progressed); and housing staffing efficiencies (£7,500, no progress). This pattern suggests stretched management and delivery resources across the council.
findings.matters: Delayed savings driven by lack of internal capacity signal stretched resources, reducing confidence in the council's ability to execute future budget plans and respond to new pressures
findings.figures: Rev&Ben3 £24,553 postponed; HSGS2 £35,000 not progressed; HSGN3 £7,500 not achieved
findings.quote: Due to capacity issues this work has not been progressed in year but will be undertaken in 26/27

findings.headline: Coach park parking schemes significantly underperforming — Wainwright Road at 13% of target, Battle at 17%
findings.detail: Two new coach parking schemes are generating only a fraction of their targets: Wainwright Road achieved £1,653 against £13,000 target (13%), Battle achieved £2,266 against £13,000 target (17%). Notes cite foreign registered vehicles and misuse of the facilities, indicating demand and enforcement challenges that were not anticipated.
findings.matters: Persistent underperformance of new parking revenue schemes suggests either weak local demand or pricing misjudgment; these are typically easier-to-predict income sources, so poor delivery indicates planning error or local economic weakness
findings.figures: Wainwright Road: target £13,000, achieved £1,653 (13%); Battle: target £13,000, achieved £2,266 (17%)
findings.quote: This is lower than anticipated in part due to foreign registered vehicles and mi-use of facility (e.g. containers without attached cab)

findings.headline: Beach Huts capital project — £115k investment undeliverable due to lack of resourcing
findings.detail: Rother planned to purchase £115,000 of beach huts as a capital project to generate revenue (20 huts × £10k purchase price plus £694/annum land lease, targeting £98,880 net saving). This was completely undeliverable and £0 was achieved. The council cites lack of available resourcing as the blocker.
findings.matters: An undeliverable capital project signals either inadequate capital access or stretched internal resources — both concerning to a lender assessing execution capability
findings.figures: Initial year project cost would be £115,000; target saving £98,880; achieved £0
findings.quote: Project undeliverable due to available resourcing

findings.headline: £453k of planned savings categorized as not anticipated to be delivered in year — 42% of total savings target
findings.detail: Rother's 2025/26 savings plan totalled £1.084m. Of this, £453,584 is explicitly categorized as not anticipated to be delivered in year. Combined with partial savings of only £45,335 achieved against £208,213 planned (22% delivery), the overall delivery is significantly weak. The council has acknowledged upfront that nearly half its savings will not materialize.
findings.matters: Savings targets this large and unachievable mid-year indicate either inadequate budget planning or deteriorating financial position — material to lender confidence in budget stability
findings.figures: Total adjusted saving budget £1,084,424; not anticipated to be delivered £453,584 (42% of total)
findings.quote: NOT ANTICIPATED TO BE DELIVERED IN YEAR £453,584 0 £0

findings.headline: Planning fee income target of £418k not delivered; council currently £440k below planning revenue target
findings.detail: Rother budgeted £418,071 in savings from planning application fee increases following government consultation, but achieved £0. Current forecasts show planning income is £440k below the full-year target. A 3.8% fee increase is planned for April 2026, but this has not yet generated the anticipated income. This is Rother's largest single saving target and the underperformance represents structural budget stress.
findings.matters: Planning income is a discretionary revenue source for councils; persistent underperformance suggests either weak development activity or demand forecasting error, both concerning to lenders
findings.figures: Agreed saving £418,071; achieved £0; current forecast £440k below full-year planning income target
findings.quote: Planning income has improved significantly compared to the 2024/25 position (expected to be an increase of £225k across the full year compared to 2024/25) but current forecasts anticipate planning income being £440k below target.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn 2025/26, Revenue and Capital Monitoring and Flexible Capital Receipts Policy
findings.headline: Hermes investment loss of £423,000 written to revenue in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The council incurred a loss on the Hermes Investment of £423,000 during the year. This loss was incorporated into the net cost of services and contributed to the overall revenue deficit position.
findings.matters: Investment losses suggest the council is taking investment risk, and this particular loss contributes to the reserve drawdown pressure.
findings.figures: Hermes investment loss: £423,000
findings.quote: The Net Cost of Services also incorporates an adverse variance to the revenue position of £1.183M in respect of a loss on the Hermes Investment of £423,000 and £759,000 of capital costs written back to revenue in year primarily in respect of the Town Hall Renaissance project and Old Lydd Rd Housing project.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn 2025/26, Revenue and Capital Monitoring and Flexible Capital Receipts Policy
findings.headline: Emerging inflation and interest rate risk flagged as negative impact on construction costs and council borrowing costs.
findings.detail: The paper identifies that the Middle East conflict is driving inflationary pressure, with living costs rising and bank and mortgage rates forecast to increase. This will increase council borrowing costs. Several significant schemes are still to be tendered (Barnhorn Green, DLWP, Sidley Waste Depot, Leisure Centre refurbishments) and if market prices exceed available budgets, further budget increases will be needed.
findings.matters: Rising interest rates directly increase the council's cost of debt. Inflationary pressure on untenderd schemes risks further budget overruns like Sidley Depot. This affects debt serviceability and capital delivery.
findings.figures: Interest paid 2025/26: £871,000; interest received: £650,000; net financing cost: £221,000
findings.quote: A new emerging risk relates to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. This is having a negative impact on inflation, with living costs rising and both bank and mortgage rates forecast to increase. If interest rates do increase, this will also have a negative impact on the Council's interest payments in respect of borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn 2025/26, Revenue and Capital Monitoring and Flexible Capital Receipts Policy
findings.headline: Total capital programme increased by £31m to £196m, driven mainly by £20m expansion of lending to housing company and £7.6m National Lottery grant for De La Warr Pavilion.
findings.detail: The capital programme has grown from a February 2025 budget of approximately £165m to £196m. The most significant movements are a £20m increase in loan provision to RDCHC (on top of the £24m drawn) and a newly awarded £7.6m National Lottery Heritage Fund grant for the De La Warr Pavilion project. Current projection for 2026/27–2029/30 spend is circa £87m.
findings.matters: A £31m programme expansion signals either rising ambition or deteriorating cost control. The RDCHC loan expansion further increases exposure to the housing company. Lenders typically scrutinise capital programme creep and related-party lending.
findings.figures: Capital programme increased from ~£165m (February 2025) to £196m (March 2026); increase £31m; RDCHC loan increase £20m; NLHF grant £7.6m; projected 2026/27–2029/30 spend £87m
findings.quote: The updated total capital budget is now £196m, which is an increase of c£31m compared to the position in February 2025. Whilst there have been various amendments during the year, the most significant movements include the increased loan provision of £20m to RDCHC, and the additional £7.6m grant award from National Lottery Heritage Fund (NLHF) in respect of the De La Warr Pavillion project.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn 2025/26, Revenue and Capital Monitoring and Flexible Capital Receipts Policy
findings.headline: Sidley Depot capital scheme forecast to cost £2.225m, a £1.15m increase from £1.075m original budget
findings.detail: The Sidley Depot originally budgeted at £1.075m is now forecast to cost £2.225m, a £1.15m overrun. The scheme was previously flagged as 'at risk' to the Corporate Programme Board due to cost estimate changes and temporary works needed to operate the food waste service from April 2026. The council is requesting additional capital approval of £0.79m and recommending funding from capital receipts.
findings.matters: A scheme flagged as at-risk with a 107% cost overrun indicates project delivery and cost control issues. Funding it from capital receipts reduces flexibility elsewhere in the programme.
findings.figures: Original budget £1.075m; revised forecast £2.225m; deficit £1.15m; additional approval requested £0.79m
findings.quote: Sidley Depot – the approved budget for the Sidley Depot development is £1.075m, this has previously been flagged as 'at risk' to the Corporate Programme Board (CPB) due to the updated cost estimates and the temporary works which were required to make the site operational for Biffa to commence the food waste service from April 2026. The budget forecast to complete the new workshop, including the interim site arrangements, is £2.225m, which leaves a budget deficit of £1.15m.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn 2025/26, Revenue and Capital Monitoring and Flexible Capital Receipts Policy
findings.headline: £24m loaned to council's housing company during the year, with auditors requiring evaluation of repayment capacity and flagging potential impact on financial position.
findings.detail: The council provided £24m in loans to RDC Housing Company during 2025/26 (a £20m increase to loan provision). The paper states that external auditors require the council to evaluate the loans annually and consider repayment capacity under the agreed terms. Critically, the paper notes this evaluation is ongoing and may affect the year-end financial position: 'This may have an impact on the year-end financial position, but it is still being evaluated.'
findings.matters: This creates significant external exposure to a related entity. If the housing company faces repayment difficulties, the council absorbs the loss, and auditor concerns about capacity suggest this is not an academic risk.
findings.figures: Loan provision during 2025/26: £24m; increase to loan provision: £20m; anticipated 2025/26 interest income from RDCHC: £1.870m
findings.quote: It should be noted the External Auditors require the Council to evaluate the loans provided to the RDCHC on an annual basis and consider any anticipated issues with their capacity for repayment under the agreed terms of the loan agreements. This may have an impact on the year-end financial position, but it is still being evaluated.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn 2025/26, Revenue and Capital Monitoring and Flexible Capital Receipts Policy
findings.headline: Budgeted savings achieved at only 44%, with £611,093 underachievement mainly from planning fee income.
findings.detail: The council set a savings target of £1,084,424 but delivered only £473,328 (44% achievement). £453,584 of savings were rated Red as not deliverable. The largest driver is planning application fee income, which fell £413,000 short of budget. The council attributes this to external economic climate and lack of capacity, factors largely outside management control.
findings.matters: Savings delivery failure suggests either weak financial planning or structural capacity issues. If income-dependent savings miss due to external factors, the council cannot rely on them in future plans.
findings.figures: Target £1,084,424; achieved £473,328; underachievement £611,093; planning fee income deficit £413,000
findings.quote: £453,584 of the savings are rated Red, as they were not deliverable in year. These largely relate to income targets which were unable to be met either due to a lack of capacity or where market forces affected the Council's ability to generate the income anticipated.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn 2025/26, Revenue and Capital Monitoring and Flexible Capital Receipts Policy
findings.headline: General Fund Reserve depleted by £1.355m, reducing from £5m to £3.65m in a single year.
findings.detail: The council budgeted for a £694k drawdown but actually drew £1.355m from reserves, a 95% overspend on the planned depletion. This reduces the general reserve by 27%. The paper itself flags this as a risk: continued reductions in reserves could lead to a s114 notice, which is the statutory mechanism for local authority financial failure.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion at this pace signals financial stress and reduces the council's buffer for unexpected costs or income shocks. A s114 notice would be a significant credit event.
findings.figures: General Fund Reserve fell from £5m (1 April 2025) to £3.65m (31 March 2026); actual drawdown £1.355m against budgeted £694k
findings.quote: The Council has a responsibility to operate within a balanced budget and maintain Reserves at an appropriate level. Continued reductions in the Council's reserves would lead to potential risks of a s114 notice.

findings.paper_title: Rother DC Housing Company Annual Governance Monitoring
findings.headline: A key financial control—updating the banking mandate—remains incomplete, eight months after internal audit recommendation.
findings.detail: Internal audit identified that RDCHC's Financial Scheme of Delegation must be updated to enable the banking mandate to be refreshed. This medium-priority recommendation has not yet been completed; the paper describes it as 'progressing' as of June 2026. Of eight audit recommendations overall, five are complete and three remain outstanding.
findings.matters: Banking mandates define payment authority; a lapsed or outdated mandate represents a control gap in segregation of duties and authorization levels.
findings.figures: 8 internal audit recommendations; 5 complete, 3 outstanding
findings.quote: recommendation 4.2 requires an update to RDCHC's Financial Scheme of Delegation to enable the banking mandate to be updated, which is progressing

findings.paper_title: Rother DC Housing Company Annual Governance Monitoring
findings.headline: External auditors raised queries on the council's 2024/25 Group Accounts, which incorporate RDCHC's figures.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton identified issues requiring clarification in the 2024/25 accounts when consolidating the housing company's results. The council reports it is working proactively with RDCHC to prepare working papers for this year's audit. RDCHC has separately appointed new external auditors for the 2025/26 accounts.
findings.matters: Query patterns on consolidated accounts can signal reporting issues, accounting control gaps, or valuation problems that affect the reliability of the council's financial statements.
findings.figures: 2024/25 Annual Accounts; new auditors appointed 2025/26
findings.quote: There were a number of resulting queries from the Council's External Auditors (Grant Thornton) in respect of the 2024/25 Annual Accounts.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit – Annual Report and Opinion 2025/26
findings.headline: One service area experienced disruption from employee with undocumented knowledge of critical systems
findings.detail: The Audit Manager notes in the overall opinion that one service area experienced 'Disruption caused by a single point of failure (i.e. where an employee, with unique, undocumented knowledge of important systems / processes has been unexpectedly absent for an extended period)'. Management is taking steps to address this, but the vulnerability remains.
findings.matters: Key person dependency without documentation of critical processes represents operational risk and continuity risk, particularly if such an employee were to leave the organization.
findings.figures: One service area affected
findings.quote: Disruption caused by a single point of failure (i.e. where an employee, with unique, undocumented knowledge of important systems / processes has been unexpectedly absent for an extended period) has also been an issue in one service area

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit – Annual Report and Opinion 2025/26
findings.headline: Housing Company Governance audit identified multiple unresolved issues despite upgrade from minimal to limited assurance since October 2023.
findings.detail: The Housing Company Governance audit reflects 'the number, and potential significance, of the issues still found at the time of the latest audit'. While many issues have since been resolved, all but three audit recommendations remain outstanding as of the report date, indicating ongoing governance challenges in this non-council entity.
findings.matters: Governance weaknesses in the housing company affect overall financial control and risk management outside the main council structure, and reflect management's effectiveness in overseeing subsidiary entities.
findings.figures: Three audit recommendations from Housing Company Governance audit remain unresolved
findings.quote: the latest assessment reflects the number, and potential significance, of the issues still found at the time of the latest audit. In summary, all but three of the audit recommendations have since been resolved

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit – Annual Report and Opinion 2025/26
findings.headline: Staff resource constraints expected to be heightened by Local Government Reorganisation, creating risk to governance and control effectiveness.
findings.detail: The Audit Manager explicitly warns in the overall opinion that 'limited staff resources have continued to be an issue in some service areas, and any resulting weaknesses in governance or internal control may only be heightened once further resources are diverted to work on Local Government Reorganisation.' This signals reduced management capacity during a critical organizational change period.
findings.matters: Reduced management capacity during reorganization could limit the council's ability to effectively manage finances, implement necessary control improvements, and respond to emerging issues.
findings.figures: Resource diversion to Local Government Reorganisation work identified as forward-looking risk
findings.quote: limited staff resources have continued to be an issue in some service areas, and any resulting weaknesses in governance or internal control may only be heightened once further resources are diverted to work on Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: Council has £35m at-risk investment in housing company with repayment dependent on open market sales
findings.detail: Rother has lent £29.15m to its housing company (RDCHC), forecast to rise to £32.3m by March 2026 and peak at £35m in June 2026. Repayment of both principal and capitalised interest depends on open market sales 'subject to market conditions.' The CFO acknowledges 'This represents a risk to the Councils budget and reserves levels, should that risk crystalise.' While there is offsetting monitoring and a pre-sale agreement with a Registered Provider, open market sales risk remains live and material.
findings.matters: This is a large contingent liability. If the housing company's open market sales falter (already subject to economic headwinds given the planning fee decline), the council could face a cliff in cash inflows and be unable to recover the loaned capital or interest.
findings.figures: £29.15m loaned to date; forecast £32.3m by 31 March 2026; £35m peak in June 2026
findings.quote: The level of loans provided to the Councils Housing Company currently stands at £29.15m and is forecast to be £32.3m by 31 March 2026. The investment is forecast to peak in June 2026 at around £35m... The repayment of the loans themselves and the capitalised interest costs due to the Council are predicted on both the income due from the sales to the open market and those to the Registered Provider. The latter is certain, but the former is subject to market conditions. This represents a risk to the Councils budget and reserves levels, should that risk crystalise.

findings.headline: Planning and building control fee income reduced by £120k due to housing downturn
findings.detail: The council has reduced its planning and building control fee income target from £1.46m (2025/26) to £1.34m (2026/27) 'due to the downturn in the housing market and general economic climate.' This demand-led income stream is vulnerable to economic cycles and will continue to be 'monitored regularly to identify any significant adverse variances.'
findings.matters: Demand-led income volatility is a warning sign. The council is already cutting its income forecast and explicitly flags this as a risk area that will need close monitoring.
findings.figures: Reduced from £1.46m to £1.34m (£120k reduction)
findings.quote: We have reduced this target to £1.34m in 2026/27 due to the downturn in the housing market and general economic climate.

findings.headline: Adjustment Support Grant continuation beyond 2026/27 is uncertain; loss would be £447k headwind in 2027/28
findings.detail: The council's funding settlement is now subject to central government confirmation of the Adjustment Support Grant beyond 2026/27. If this grant is not continued, the council's funding picture in 2027/28 will be £447k worse than currently projected, and a further £420k worse in 2028/29. This uncertainty compounds the deficits already forecast.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know what portion of the council's funding is contingent on policy decisions outside its control. The loss of £447k would widen a predicted deficit and force larger reserve drawdowns.
findings.figures: £447,000 worse in 2027/28 if Adjustment Support Grant is not continued; £420,000 further impact in 2028/29
findings.quote: If the Adjustment Support Grant is not continued over the term of the MTFP then the funding picture in 2027/8 will be £447,000 worse than reported (& a further £420,000 in 2028/29).

findings.headline: Homelessness and temporary accommodation costs have more than tripled in four years and now stand at £3.1m
findings.detail: The council is facing runaway demand-led costs in homelessness and temporary accommodation, now budgeted at approximately £3.1m—more than triple the level of four years ago. The CFO identifies this as a 'significant demand led budget pressure' and acknowledges the activity that drives costs 'remains difficult to predict.' This is the largest demand-led risk on the council's balance sheet.
findings.matters: Homelessness costs are volatile, often statutory, and can force emergency reserve drawdowns. Tripling in four years signals structural demand that is unlikely to reverse and exposes the council to further pressures.
findings.figures: c£3.1m budgeted for 2026/27; more than tripled over four years
findings.quote: The Council is experiencing significant demand led budget pressures, particularly in respect of homelessness and temporary accommodation costs which are now budgeted at c£3.1m and more than have tripled over the last four years.

findings.headline: Pay award negotiations pose £920k unaffordable risk if union claims are met
findings.detail: The council budgeted 3% for staff pay rises, but NJC negotiations opened at least £3,000 or 10% whichever is greater—the CFO explicitly calls these 'unaffordable for the Council and would represent a significant risk to our financial sustainability if agreed.' The additional cost would be approximately £920k above the 3% provision. A multi-year settlement could cost even more (RPI+3% for year 2, RPI+2% for year 3). No agreement has been reached and negotiations may take months.
findings.matters: This is a live, material budget risk that could force the council to draw on reserves mid-year or cut services. It also signals the council has limited headroom for wage pressures.
findings.figures: £920k additional cost if NJC claim is met; 3% was budgeted (c£126k per 1% increase)
findings.quote: Clearly these proposals are unaffordable for the Council and would represent a significant risk to our financial sustainability if agreed. The anticipated additional cost (over the provisional already made in the 2026/27 draft budget for a 3% uplift) would be approximately £920k.

findings.headline: Council has exhausted internal borrowing and is now externally borrowing with £7m more planned
findings.detail: The council has run out of internal cash reserves to fund capital projects and the housing company loan. Over the last 12 months it has become increasingly dependent on external borrowing. It is forecasting a further £7m of external borrowing to support £40m of capital spend over 2026/27–2028/29, though it notes it is 'not currently in a position to materially extend its capital programme if those schemes were not supported by grant funding or available capital receipts.'
findings.matters: A lender needs clarity on the council's cash position and borrowing trajectory. The shift to external borrowing exposes the council to interest rate risk at a time when PWLB rates remain elevated.
findings.figures: £7m of further borrowing forecast for £40m of scheme costs over 2026/27–2028/29
findings.quote: the Council has now exhausted its ability to internally borrowing and over the last 12 months has become increasingly reliant on needing to externally borrow

findings.headline: General reserves forecast to fall from £10.655m (March 2025) to £1.2m (March 2029); council faces £357k deficit 2027/28 and £923k deficit 2028/29
findings.detail: The council has set a balanced budget for 2026/27 but the CFO explicitly warns that the council 'remains on a path whereby reserves will be significantly depleted over the term of the MTFP.' General reserves are forecast to fall from £10.655m (March 2025) to £2.1m (March 2028) to £1.2m (March 2029). The council will have deficits of £357k in 2027/28 and £923k in 2028/29 that will be funded from reserves.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council is burning through financial buffers and will have no reserves left within three years. This is structural insolvency risk.
findings.quote: the Council remains on a path whereby reserves will be significantly depleted over the term of the MTFP

findings.paper_title: Budget & Council Tax Resolution 2026/27 and Medium-Term Financial Plan 2026-2029
findings.headline: Parish and Town Council precepts jumped 19.32%, significantly above the district council's own 2.99% increase
findings.detail: Parish and Town Council precepts across Rother rose from £4,135,044 to £4,978,213 (£843,169 increase), with average Band D contribution increasing from £104.19 to £124.31. This substantially outpaces Rother's own modest 2.99% increase and drives a cumulative 5.45% overall Band D tax rise for residents.
findings.matters: A 19% parish precept increase in one year signals compressed finances across the wider local authority structure and indicates cost pressures affecting councils' satellite bodies. Residents face rising total tax burden regardless of Rother's own restraint.
findings.quote: The Parish and Town Council Precepts (including Special Expenses for Bexhill and Rye) for 2026/27 are detailed in Appendix C and total £4,978,213 (2025/26 £4,135,044). The increase results in an average Band D Council Tax figure of £124.31 (£104.19 for 2025/26).

findings.paper_title: Budget & Council Tax Resolution 2026/27 and Medium-Term Financial Plan 2026-2029
findings.headline: Fair Funding Reform cuts Revenue Support Grant by £487,000 in 2026/27, with the offset grant only lasting one year
findings.detail: The government's amended business rates retention methodology reduces Rother's RSG by £487,000 in 2026/27. This is offset by the 'Adjustment Support Grant' for that year only. From 2027/28 onwards, unless the situation changes, the council faces a £487,000 structural funding gap that must be managed through savings, service reduction, or reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: A temporary funding offset creates a forward budget cliff in 2027/28. Lenders assess three-year forward positions; a known future cut of this magnitude reduces the council's financial headroom and may force strategic choices about service levels or borrowing.
findings.figures: £487,000 RSG reduction, offset by 'Adjustment Support Grant' of the same value in 2026/27 only
findings.quote: The Fair Funding Reform redistribution of Business Rates retention methodology was amended from the provisional settlement, which resulted in the Council receiving £487,000 less Revenue Support Grant (RSG) funding than previously anticipated in 2026/27.  In 2026/27 only this will be offset by the 'Adjustment Support Grant' of the same value.

findings.paper_title: Summary of Debt Management framework and write-offs
findings.headline: Housing accounts for 70% of write-offs by count (117 of 168) and 74% by value (£45,707 of £61,432), all homelessness-related.
findings.detail: The majority of debts written off related to Housing homelessness cases, predominantly because customers entered Individual Voluntary Arrangements (IVAs), had no fixed abode and no means to pay, lacked documentation, or the debt was aged. All 117 Housing write-offs came from this single service line.
findings.matters: A concentration of uncollectible debt in one service reflects either high-need client bases unable to pay or structural collection issues within that service.
findings.figures: 117 debts written off (69.6% of 168), £45,707 (74.4% of £61,432 total)
findings.quote: The majority of the debts written off (117) related to the Housing Service, which all related to homelessness cases. The reasons for write off varied, but were predominantly due to the customer entering into an IVA (Individual Voluntary Arrangement), being of no fixed abode and no means to pay, lack of record retention or the age of the debt.

findings.paper_title: Summary of Debt Management framework and write-offs
findings.headline: The Debt Management Framework was removed from the Council's Constitution and is only now being formally re-documented.
findings.detail: Recent versions of the Financial Procedure Rules dropped the detailed Debt Management Policy that was historically included. The council is now creating updated process notes and refreshing the framework, with completion scheduled for May 2026. Officer delegations are being reviewed concurrently.
findings.matters: A gap in formally documented governance and controls for debt management, even if being remedied, indicates the council operates without explicit written procedures for an important financial process.
findings.figures: Scheduled completion May 2026; timing of when framework was removed from Constitution not specified
findings.quote: More recently adopted versions of the Financial Procedure Rules have not contained this level of detail, but work is being undertaken on ensuring that a defined set of process notes is available for staff, and an updated version of the Debt Management Framework is scheduled to be drafted by May.

findings.paper_title: Summary of Debt Management framework and write-offs
findings.headline: Three COVID-related Estates debts totaling £27,739 remain unresolved with decisions pending past the pandemic.
findings.detail: One of the three COVID Estates debts has been paid by the lessor. One is recommended for write-off but awaiting further details from the Head of Finance. A third is subject to an ongoing rent review being assessed by the new Strategic Assets and Estates Manager, with the proposed action to be outlined ahead of the financial year end depending on the outcome of rent negotiations.
findings.matters: Lingering pandemic-era lease and property debts still on the balance sheet over two years later, with one pending a renegotiation outcome, indicate ongoing balance-sheet drag from COVID.
findings.figures: £27,739 in three related debts; one remaining debt recommended for write-off pending review; final resolution date not specified beyond 'financial year end'
findings.quote: One debt has been recommended for write off due to the tenant's financial standing, however further details were sought by the Head of Finance, and those are awaited. The third debt is subject to an ongoing rent review; this account is currently being assessed by the new Strategic Assets and Estates Manager, and they will be outlining the proposed action to the Head of Housing and Strategic Assets and Director of Resources ahead of the financial year end, depending on the outcome of the ongoing negotiations.

findings.detail: The Risk Management section states: 'Continued reductions in the Council's reserves would lead to potential risks of a Section 114 Notice.' A Section 114 notice prevents the council from spending on anything except statutory functions.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a severe governance failure that would materially affect service delivery and the council's creditworthiness.

findings.quote: Continued reductions in the Council's reserves would lead to potential risks of a Section 114 Notice

findings.headline: Business Rates reset in 2026/27 will eliminate all accumulated growth and redistribute it; pool arrangements uncertain
findings.detail: A full Business Rates reset for 2026/27 means all growth accumulated to date is subject to redistribution across the sector, with only new growth post-reset retained by individual councils. Rother is part of a Business Rates Pool with other East Sussex authorities; the Government is currently reviewing pool arrangements and mechanics. Multiplier changes are also planned.
findings.matters: Elimination of historic growth removes income upside the council may have been relying on, and uncertainty about pool arrangements creates unquantifiable forecast risk.
findings.figures: Full Business Rates reset 2026/27; all accumulated growth subject to redistribution
findings.quote: This reset will be a full reset, which means that all growth accumulated to date is potentially subject to redistribution across the sector for future periods, and only new growth gained after the reset will be retained

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review 2.0 from 2026/27 will reduce Rother's funding as money redistributes to higher-deprivation areas
findings.detail: The Government's Fair Funding Review explicitly redistributes funding from lower to higher-deprivation areas. Rother, as a lower-deprivation council, will see funding shift away. The council states: 'This will mean for authorities such as Rother District Council that we will not see funding levels rise in line with inflationary pressures faced.' The multi-year settlement provides real-terms growth only for councils with social care responsibilities (county and unitaries), not district councils.
findings.matters: Unlike many councils seeing real-terms growth, Rother faces a structural squeeze where Government funding cannot keep pace with inflation, making service cuts more severe.
findings.figures: Fair Funding Review 2.0 implementation 2026/27; multi-year settlement with 3-year transitional arrangements
findings.quote: This will mean for authorities such as Rother District Council that we will not see funding levels rise in line with inflationary pressures faced. The shift of funding towards those areas of high deprivation will also see funding shifted over the multi-year settle period

findings.detail: Planning income baseline is being permanently reduced by £119,000 as part of growth items for consultation. This reflects reduced volumes of applications being received, not a pricing or policy change, indicating a structural loss of revenue-raising capacity.
findings.matters: A permanent reduction in the income base is harder to recover than a temporary shortfall and constrains the council's future financial flexibility.

findings.quote: Reduction in baseline Planning Income due to volume of applications received 119,000

findings.headline: Current year overspend of £250,000 combined with £1.32m in reserve impacts reducing General Reserve from £5m to potentially £2.7m
findings.detail: 2025/26 shows a revenue overspend of £250,000 driven by planning income shortfall, estates voids and agency staff costs. The General Reserve is already being drawn down by £694,000 in the budget. Additionally, the council has suffered a £420,000 loss on the Hermes Property Fund and faces potential £900,000 loss from aborted capital schemes, which collectively could reduce the General Reserve to £2.7m.
findings.matters: Multiple simultaneous reserve impacts significantly reduce the council's financial buffer and heighten Section 114 risk, particularly concerning during LGR transition when scrutiny is heightened.

news_drafts.headline: Rother's reserves forecast to halve despite balancing immediate budget
news_drafts.lead: Rother District Council approved a balanced budget for 2026/27 without drawing on reserves, reversing two years in which it had relied on reserves to close budget gaps. However, auditors have flagged that the council's reserves are forecast to decline from £2.5 million in 2026/27 to £1.2 million by March 2029 — a 52 per cent fall. Auditors identify this as the most significant risk to the council's medium-term financial resilience, compounded by a material factor: the council's £35.6 million loan to Rother DC Housing Company, which matures in March 2028. As at July 2026, only three of 200 planned homes had been completed and none sold. The council also achieved only 44 per cent of a £1.1 million savings target in 2025/26, compared with 87 per cent the prior year, due to shortfalls in income-generation schemes.
